items.title: Why some regional brokerages are avoiding ancillary services
items.description: It's no secret that the U.S. housing market may see fewer than 4 million existing home sales in 2027. In an attempt to boost ever-tightening margins and claim a larger slice of the transaction pie, many large national brokerages have spent the past year doubling down on ancillary services. From new mortgage joint ventures to diving into mortgage servicing , companies from eXp Realty to HomeServices of America are looking to further integrate the disparate parts of a real estate transaction into one vertical platform. While this may be the way some of the nation’s largest brokerage companies are thinking about the future, many regional brokerages with strong market share in their states or metros are taking a different tack. “Our company has been around for 153 years and our strategy has always been to be masters of our craft and not to chase every adjacent revenue stream,” Matt Leone, the chief marketing officer at Brown Harris Stevens (BHS), a RealTrends Verified brokerage, said. “I think that we are a residential resale, new development and property management brokerage. Mortgage and title may offer additional income, but our greatest opportunity is to stay relentlessly focused on real estate and be the best at that. I think, when you venture into other arenas, your core gets saturated and your eyes come off the prize.” Like BHS, Linda O’Koniewski ’s RealTrends Verified firm, Leading Edge Real Estate , is also staying out of ancillary services. “While margins are critically thin for brokerages, and the income would be welcome, we have given it all up,” O’Koniewski said, noting that her company had previously had partnerships with insurance and mortgage companies. “What our clients need is the best loan officer and product. They need a super-responsive insurance agent. We are dedicating ourselves to developing processes and strategies that pre-resolve preventable problems in a transaction and create the best outcomes for our clients.” O’Koniewski added that her firm’s in-house legal counsel has also suggested homing in on real estate as industries like mortgage and title are not their primary area of expertise. Although firms like Leading Edge and BHS may not own or have ancillary services joint ventures, this doesn’t mean they lack relationships with lenders or title companies. Advertising services not ancillary services At BHS, instead of offering mortgage or title services directly or through a joint venture, the company works with trusted mortgage or title professionals to contribute to the company’s blog, sponsor its podcasts and participate in educational panel discussions. Leone said BHS works to establish relationships with the top mortgage and title professionals through a “massive in-house commitment to marketing and content creation,” bringing voices from ancillary services industries that BHS feels are the most aligned with its culture and mission. “They're providing their expertise to our audience that follows us, as well as providing advertising support to expand the audience that views our 18-plus podcasts and in-house created episodic series shows,” he said. “It is legitimate advertising and earned media exposure at fair market value that allows us to get their expertise to broadcast that to our client base and it also allows us to have an ancillary source of legitimate income.” Through these posts and marketing material, Leone said BHS is looking to educate its agents and clients, which is why the brokerage likes to partner with creative and experienced ancillary services providers through the program. “We're bringing experienced professionals that have seen it all before, and we like to bring those individuals in to get their insights,” Leone said. “Hopefully it allows everyone to stay informed and that is our goal when we're creating content.” While not yet as advanced as BHS’s marketing machine, this is what Peter Voss is looking to do with the in-house video production and editing segment he and his team have launched at 3% Listing Co . “Agents can schedule a time with the in-house video team whenever they want and work with our director on a script and then get in front of the camera and record. We take care of all the editing and produce the video,” Voss said. Voss said, for his firm, the video production started as a way to provide services to their agents that are beneficial to their business, but also something his firm could afford without significantly increasing overhead costs. “It is a way to help our agents get their branding out and hopefully generate more transactions, which helps them but also helps our business,” he said. In the future, Voss said they are looking to expand this service beyond just 3% Listing Co agents, allowing the company to have an additional revenue stream similar to BHS’s operation. While brokerages like BHS, 3% Listing Co. and Leading Edge may not feel the need to go all-in on ancillary services, Michele Harrington , at First Team Real Estate , a RealTrends Verified firm, sees them as a must-have. Are ancillary services a ‘no-brainer?’ “It is kind of a no-brainer. The profit margins in the real estate brokerage business are just so tiny, so any little bump in the market or a downturn in the market is really going to hurt,” Harrington, a HousingWire Woman of Influence , said. This is why Harrington believes anyone who owns a brokerage should be exploring ancillary services. items.title: Will the AI stock sell-off give us sub-7% mortgage rates before the holidays?
items.description: Sub-7% mortgage rates are back on the holiday menu! Just when it looked like we had no chance for a happy holiday, AI stocks are still taking a beating and pushing money into bonds. Oil prices almost went below $80 last week too. We have three holidays left before 2027 kicks into gear, so the question now is: Can we get the 10-year yield and mortgage spreads low enough to get lower mortgage rates ? 10-year yield and mortgage rates In the 2026 HousingWire forecast , I anticipated the following ranges: Mortgage rates between 5.75% and 6.75% The 10-year yield fluctuating between 3.80% and 4.60% If all this market drama happened four weeks ago, I believe the 10-year yield would be under 4.85% today, but this is happening amid a rapid-fire, two-week effort by the Federal Reserve to give forward-guidance about more rate hikes coming in the system. The key level of 5.15% for the 10-year yield held last week, and with the AI sell-off and oil prices down to $83 again, we have a shot to get sub-7% mortgage rates again, but that will require the 10-year yield to get to 4.85% and head lower — and for mortgage spreads to improve back down toward 2%. Mortgage rates have had a difficult time lately with the inflation data and the Fed's hawkish tone. In addition, we still don’t have a resolution to the Iran conflict, and when President Trump talks about bigger tariffs with our partners, it makes it harder for yields to go down. We also have to be mindful that inflation is rising while the unemployment rate is falling; if those two things change, it will be better for rates. For now, let’s focus on getting rates lower before the holidays. What can get us there? 1. Stocks selling off almost got us to 4.85% again; we got as low as 4.92% Friday. The problem is the speed of the decline doesn’t help mortgage spreads. However, if we see more market selling, that can be one positive variable. 2. Any positive news on the Iran conflict or limiting the trade war. 3. The hope that the Democrats will resolve the conflict and trade war after Jan. 3 might get bond traders and oil traders thinking differently. We don’t have much time before the end-of-year holidays, but the above will help. However, the reverse is also true: stocks rallying, the conflict getting worse or more negative trade war headlines can lead yields and rates higher. Mortgage spreads Mortgage spreads have recently gotten worse, which is a big variable in why rates got as high as 7.60% recently, but they’re still close to multiyear lows. We need less volatility in the bond markets, and with time, the spreads can improve again. Since September, the markets have been a bit too wild, rising and falling, and the spreads' job is to reduce mortgage rate volatility. A big key for mortgage rates to get below 7% is getting the spreads back to 2% and under. Historically, mortgage spreads have ranged from 1.60% to 1.80%. Last week, spreads rose to 2.18% from 2.15% a week earlier. Let’s compare last week’s mortgage rates to where they would have been at the best spread levels this year and the worst levels of this cycle. If we had the best levels of spreads in 2026, mortgage rates would be 6.96% today, not 7.33% . If we had the worst mortgage spread levels of 2023, mortgage rates would be 8.26% today. Weekly pending sales Our pending home sales data provides a week-to-week perspective, though holidays and short-term fluctuations can affect results. This weekly pending sales data typically takes 30-60 days to reflect in sales data. We saw slight week-to-week growth last week and housing data has really stabilized in the recent weeks; however, I would just view this as an adjustment to the rate shock we saw when rates moved from 6.75% to 7.60%, and demand got noticeably hit. The year-over-year comps are going to be difficult for some time, as mortgage rates were much lower last year than today. Here are the pending sales for last week over the last two years: 2026: 53,490 2025: 58,612 Purchase applications Purchase application data, which looks out 30-90 days, has softened as mortgage rates rose above 6.64% and are now above 7%. Rates rose aggressively during inflation week, so this data line did get hit, down 3% week-to-week and down 18% year-over-year. Again, the year-over-year comps here are rough, as mortgage rates were a lot lower last year. Earlier in the year, all we had was positive year-over-year, but rates reached the range where housing data slows down, and the comps have been very difficult. Here are the stats on purchase apps so far in 2026: 17 positive week-to-week prints 25 negative week-to-week prints 5 flat week-to-week prints 10 weeks of double-digit year-over-year growth 25 weeks of positive year-over-year growth 17 negative year-over-year prints Housing inventory Housing inventory had a slight decline last week and is in its seasonal decline for 2026, as the peak in inventory already happened. Inventory growth did pick up when mortgage rates headed toward 7.60%; before that, inventory growth was slow this year, and we even had some weeks when inventory was negative year-over-year. Until mid-June it was hard for the comps to show growth this year and now they’re much easier to show growth as housing demand was heading toward a nine-month high last year this time. items.title: Why aren’t mortgage rates lower after massive stock sell-off?
items.description: AI stocks have sold off and oil prices are lower, but the 10-year yield is at 4.94% and mortgage rates are still abouve 7.30%. So what gives? The Federal Reserve has been worried about oil prices driving inflation since the Iran conflict began and has noted that the trade war inflation has mostly been passed through. Now AI stocks are being slammed, with moratoriums on data centers coming in the near future as the anti-AI backlash grows. In this environment, you could expect the 10-year yield and rates to fall, but that's not what's happening. I talked about this on the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor-in-Chief Sarah Wheeler, but with today’s market action, I need to revisit this question with some charts. Let’s go over each part of this storyline. Oil prices Oil prices were very volatile earlier this year and bond yields started moving in synch with them — especially after the first MOU deal broke off . Now that oil prices have fallen, you might expect at least a few Federal Reserve members to say that this could be a positive, but they haven’t. In fact, when oil was trading between $68-$82, no Fed members said anything positive, and Cleveland Fed President (and Fed hawk ) Beth Hammack talked about how lower oil prices were were actually bad for inflation because people could then spend more money. In any case, so far, lower oil prices haven’t helped the 10-year yield get below 4.70%. If oil can trade between $67-$82, that would help a lot, but the last time that happened was when we announced a deal with Iran in June. AI stocks I have used the CoreWeave stock price as an example of the problems with the AI companies. Since CoreWeave had some financing issues, the markets have soured on AI, and as you can see in the chart below, the company’s stock price has been crushed. This has helped keep the 10-year yield below 5.35% for sure and has assisted in lower yields this week. But we are still elevated versus what we saw after the MOU deal was announced. The Fed has made AI a huge inflation talking point, and they need to see much more pain in the AI sector before changing their tune. Fed went into hawkish overdrive If we were getting all this news about AI and oil prices four weeks ago, I believe the 10-year yield and mortgage rates would be lower today. But all this stock drama and falling oil prices came in a 14-day period where the Fed hawks came out every day talking about more Fed rate hikes, even a 50-basis-point hike. I mean, look at how the U.S. dollar hasn’t been fazed by the market drama. 10-year yield bounced off key support line For the past two months, I have focused on two key levels for the 10-year yield: 5.35% and 5.15%. Both those levels held and yields have fallen from these points. So what lower oil prices and falling stocks have done is made sure bond yields don’t go much higher and for now, let's take that as a victory. However, I do understand why people might be scratching their heads on why rates aren't lower with lower oil prices and falling AI stocks. Conclusion The Fed hawks are the main reason bond yields aren’t lower; they want to make sure that the bond market doesn’t get relaxed, even with lower oil prices and falling stocks, and they have done their job well. They really want to take back all the insurance interest rate cuts from last year and because of this, the 10-year yield is still at 4.95%. If the Fed members weren’t so hawkish over the last two weeks, bond yields would be lower and we would have already had sub-7% mortgage rates . Related More:

items.title: Homebuilders' $30B buying spree has cooled; now it's all execution
items.description: For the better part of 15 years, U.S. homebuilding has been on a mergers-and-acquisitions buying spree. Since 2010, more than 200 homebuilder transactions have conservatively totaled more than $30 billion in announced deal value, based on just seven of the largest acquisitions and excluding scores of private-company transactions whose purchase prices were never disclosed. The buying continued through 2026, with Berkshire Hathaway 's $8.5 billion acquisition of Taylor Morrison and Sumitomo Forestry 's approximately $4.5 billion purchase of Tri Pointe Homes among the year's largest deals. More recent transactions included Daiwa House subsidiary Stanley Martin 's July acquisition of Holiday Builders , Dream Finders Homes ' August acquisition of Beazer Home s, and Century Communities' October purchase of HistoryMaker Homes . Yet even as those transactions have reshaped the industry's competitive landscape, the economics of homebuilding have shifted . Weak demand, costly sales incentives, shrinking margins, and uncertainty over land and home values are forcing acquirers to reconsider not only which businesses are worth buying but also how the companies they already own should operate . "We're not busy now," one deeply experienced homebuilding M&A dealmaker told me recently. "This is no time to be trying to take a seller to market for acquisition. Nothing's happening." That assessment does not mean homebuilding consolidation has ended. It’s still “morning time in America” for homebuilding’s inevitable grind toward concentration of fewer, ever larger, more industrialized homebuilding giants. My source’s observation suggests that the economics of bringing new sellers to market have become harder, even as the largest and best-capitalized acquirers continue pursuing strategic combinations. Business and investment models in homebuilding can look remarkably good when demand, prices, and asset values are rising. The real test comes when the cycle turns, gravity takes hold, and assumptions that worked on the way up begin to break down. That's when the industry's outliers distinguish themselves, not simply through stronger balance sheets, but by how well their people work together, how quickly they adapt their processes, how effectively they serve customers, and how consistently they outperform competitors when business conditions get messy. That is the test now confronting the companies assembled through homebuilding's extraordinary consolidation era. Have their acquisitions produced merely bigger enterprises, or have they developed the leadership, operating discipline, local knowledge, and capacity to improve that will make them fundamentally better homebuilders with greater connectivity to and attainability for America’s economically bifurcated households? The answer will increasingly depend on what happens inside the enterprises they've acquired. The challenge is to capture the value of their land positions while developing the people, operating systems, technologies, and organizational capabilities needed to replenish those positions, improve profitability, and serve customers more efficiently in a difficult market likely to extend into 2027 and potentially 2028. That is where the next, and perhaps most demanding, phase of homebuilding consolidation begins. What the buyers actually bought Homebuilding acquisitions are distinct from many other corporate combinations because the value of the acquired business is inseparable from its land positions and the people capable of turning those positions – sustainably and repeatedly – into profitable homes. An attractive acquisition may bring years of controlled lots, entitled development opportunities, established relationships with landowners and municipalities, and access to markets that would take an outsider years to enter. It may also include an experienced management team, trusted trade relationships, established brands and the organizational knowledge and local intel needed to perpetuate the business beyond its current land pipeline. Those assets are related, but they are not interchangeable. When one goes missing, the others quickly fall out of balance. The value of the land depends on its location, basis, development requirements, timing, and the demand for homes that can be built on it profitably. Realizing that value depends on decisions about product, construction costs, sales strategy, purchasing, development sequencing, and capital allocation. An acquirer that buys a good land portfolio but loses the ability to develop and replenish it efficiently may find that the acquisition's original promise was a mere blip. An acquirer that preserves an admired local management organization without improving its operating economics may find that the business remains well regarded yet increasingly uncompetitive. Successful acquisitions require balancing those two realities. The objective is to capture the value of the acquired land and operating platform as a launching pad for building the leadership, relationships, systems, and financial discipline needed to extend that profitability long after the original inventory has been delivered. That balance of 100% binding capabilities becomes harder to hold together when market conditions weaken. When integration becomes unavoidable For years, one of the most attractive features of selling to Berkshire Hathaway's Clayton Properties Group or one of the major Japan-based acquirers was the prospect of continuity. Many regional builders joined larger, well-capitalized ownership organizations while retaining key elements of their identities, management teams, local relationships, and operating independence. That approach appealed to owners seeking liquidity or a succession solution without losing the character of the companies they had built. It also made strategic sense. items.title: Howard Hanna sued over $395 real estate transaction fee
items.description: Howard Hanna Real Estate Services is joining the growing roster of real estate firms facing a lawsuit over a “transaction fee” a consumer was allegedly forced to pay in conjunction with their real estate transaction. Earlier this month, first-time homebuyer Dena Bergamasco filed a suit against Howard Hanna over a $395 “Realtor Transaction Fee” she claims she was charged on top of the buyer broker commission she paid related to her October 2021 home purchase. Bergamasco is being represented by Kopelowitz Ostrow P.A. one of the firms representing plaintiff Gregory Deivert in his transaction fee lawsuit filed against a Keller Williams franchise last month. Attorneys for Bergamasco claim in the filing that as her buyer broker Howard Hanna breached its fiduciary duty and violated the state’s Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law in charging her this fee, which the suit describes as a “cash grab.” Bargamasco claims that the $395 fee was charged “for nothing” with “no service behind it, no cost behind it, and no name that accurately describes it.” “It is money taken from a client by the broker who was supposed to be looking out for her,” the complaint states. According to the complaint, the fee was “wedged” between third-party charges for a pest inspection fee and an owner's title insurance premium in the closing disclosure. Additionally, the complaint alleges that the brokerage coaches agents to tell clients that the fee is mandatory and serves a “processing” or “administrative” purpose. In the filing, Bergamasco’s attorneys state that she paid $217,000 for her home, with $213,069 of this coming from a federally insured mortgage and $10,850 coming from a second loan from the Pennsylvania Housing Finance Agency. In addition to this, the sellers awarded her a $7,300 credit to use toward closing costs. In total, the filing states that Bergamasco brought $788.95 in cash to her closing, not even double the cost of the alleged fee. According to the filing, with the home purchase transaction occurring prior to the Sitzer/Burnett commission lawsuit settlement , the plaintiff’s buyer broker commission was paid by the home seller and that Bergamasco paid for the paperwork completed by the settlement agent and title insurance provider at the closing. The suit is seeking class action status and the plaintiff has demanded a jury trial. Bergamasco said she is seeking damages and a permanent injunction preventing Howard Hanna from charging this fee in the future. Howard Hanna did not immediately return HousingWire’ s request for comment regarding the lawsuit. The complaint claims that the practice of charging consumers a “transaction fee” is not unique to Howard Hanna. This is evidenced in the other lawsuits that have popped up this year, including the lawsuit against Keller Williams Elite over an alleged $650 “broker fee” and a since voluntarily dismissed lawsuit filed against Compass over an alleged $475 transaction fee. Some reports, such as one from the Consumer Policy Center , claim that consumers pay up to $2 billion in brokerage transaction fees each year. items.title: The Blue Wave Has Foreign Capital Dipping Its Toes Back Into U.S. Commercial Real Estate
items.description: Trade wars , inflation and prolonged conflict in the Middle East made foreign investors increasingly cautious about the U.S., even as cross-border transactions rebounded globally. But in the aftermath of Democratic Party victories in midterm elections across the country, overseas capital may once again be warming to American real estate, fund managers said at Bisnow ’s New York City State of the Market event on Thursday. Unsplash/Amelia “The sentiment toward the U.S. was very, very negative, and even since two weeks ago, we've seen some thawing in those pools of capital that were pulling back from the U.S. for the past couple of years,” Vistria Group partner Sherry Wang said onstage. That marks a sharp reversal from earlier this year, when Wang said some foreign funds rescinded mandates to invest in the U.S., citing geopolitical concerns even as they continued to “believe in the underlying real estate for the most part.” In the first half of the year, cross-border investment in commercial real estate surged 56% to $71.8B globally, Reuters reported . Most of that increase came from Asia and Europe. Singapore ranked first among individual markets, attracting $8.7B in investment. The U.S. captured a smaller-than-usual slice of the global market. In the 12 months leading up to September, the country attracted $28B, a 15% share of all cross-border investment, according to a report by Colliers . That lagged below its five-year average of nearly 19%. Between 2022 and 2024, many investors held allocations in the U.S. steady, before decreasing their targets by 10 basis points in 2025, according to the Association of Foreign Investors in Real Estate . In an AFIRE survey conducted throughout July and August, 53% of respondents, representing more than $4T in global assets, said they plan to decrease or not change their overall U.S. allocations. That’s even though 58% of those same respondents had a positive view of the U.S. economy. Those with a negative outlook more than doubled from the same time last year, from 12.5% to nearly 27%, with more than 90% of respondents citing the U.S. political landscape as the reason why. Bisnow/Sasha Jones Cole Schotz’s Robert DiPisa, Besen Partners’ Sam Finkler, Legal 1031 Exchange’s Todd Pajonas, Muss Development’s Jason Muss and Vistria Group’s Sherry Wang Few of the factors that stood in the way of dealmaking — like interest rates and construction costs — have changed since Election Day, but there is a greater sense of certainty and, in some parts of the U.S. economy, positivity. In its first survey since the midterms , Oxford Economics found that U.S. consumer sentiment rose and year-ahead inflation expectations fell by a full percentage point to 3.7%, the most substantial decline since the start of the Iran war . Having a blue Congress and a red White House is likely to create new hurdles that block laws, budgets or appointments from approval. For the real estate industry, that may not be such a bad thing, Legal 1031 Exchange President Todd Pajonas said during the event, held at Convene One Liberty Plaza. “There's not going to be any change to the tax code, which drives a lot of business. There's not going to be huge swings in monetary policy. We're not going to see the huge tariffs . We're going to see an end, hopefully, to the conflict in the Middle East because there's not going to be the political will to do it,” Pajonas said. “I think the next two years are going to look somewhat better because of political gridlock.” AFIRE CEO Gunnar Branson told GlobeSt earlier this month that his members expressed a similar sentiment to him on the day of the election. Real estate played a prominent role in November’s election, with housing affordability and data center backlash taking center stage. Across the country, a series of Republican stronghold states flipped, including Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska, in some cases giving Democrats control for the first time in decades . In New York City, where several candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America won, landlords especially fear tightening tenant protections. “You look at COPA , that was just enacted. Every now and then — I don't even want to say it out loud — the commercial rent control bill rears its ugly head,” Besen Partners Managing Director Sam Finkler said. “It's really local policy agenda and interest rates that are going to play out over the next couple of years.” Bisnow/Sasha Jones Adler & Stachenfeld’s Kim Le, BGO’s Abbe Franchot Borok, Silverstein Properties’ Jeffrey Deitrich, Pimco's Michael Givner and NAI Global’s Arthur Milston Even with increased regulatory scrutiny, New York City continues to be one of the most supply-constrained markets in the country. Foreign investors may take a moment to recalibrate, but they are unlikely to be dissuaded in the long run, panelists said. “I don't think there's any foreign capital that has redlined, crossed off New York because of the political climate,” NAI Global Senior Managing Director and Head of Capital Markets Arthur Milston said. “In fact, I think most people view that typically as transient.” Manhattan’s median rent reached $5,279 per month in October, up 6% year-over-year, while vacancy fell to 1.3%, the lowest level since March 2020, according to Corcoran . The city has led the country in office recovery and is one of the few markets where new office supply is being delivered. Globally, the under-construction office pipeline was 580M SF in the third quarter, 45% below its 2017 peak and its lowest level in a decade, according to Cushman & Wakefield . items.title: HUD Issues Final Citizenship Rule, Giving Landlords Just Weeks To Comply
items.description: Landlords will be forced to start ejecting most immigrants who can’t prove they’re U.S. citizens from federally funded housing in early 2027 or risk losing subsidies, under a new rule from the Department of Housing and Urban Development . Bisnow/Emily Wishingrad As many as 200,000 residents are no longer eligible to stay in properties that receive HUD funding, according to a final rule released by the department this month. The change is intended to ensure that noncitizens who don’t meet the criteria to live in HUD-funded housing move elsewhere, freeing up housing for American families, the Trump administration said earlier this year when announcing the policy. But removing immigrants from federally subsidized homes will likely result in less subsidy for landlords and less housing supply, housing advocates told Bisnow . “This is going to reduce funding for housing,” said Marie Claire Tran-Leung , evictions initiative project director and managing attorney at the National Housing Law Project . “It will apply to millions of people, including citizens who live in and receive assistance from the biggest housing programs that the federal government provides.” In January, HUD announced that a large swath of residents in HUD-assisted housing will no longer receive the department’s help to pay rent. The only people who will be eligible are U.S. citizens and those who are part of a short list of noncitizens, including green card holders and asylum seekers. Other tenants who may be eligible but are without documentation will have to leave, and household members who do not receive subsidies will have to split up from those who do. The department released its finalized rule on Nov. 10, along with an updated estimate of around 19,660 tenants in HUD-assisted housing who don't have proper documentation. The rule affects public housing authorities and landlords whose tenants receive other HUD rental assistance . “President Trump warned that the days of illegal aliens and ineligible noncitizens exploiting government-funded welfare programs would be over,” HUD Secretary Scott Turner said in a statement . “It’s unacceptable that America’s homeless veterans, disabled, elderly, and victims of domestic violence languish on waitlists while illegals and ineligibles scam our system.” All tenants in HUD -assisted housing must now prove that they are either U.S. citizens or fall into one of the categories of immigrants who are eligible to live in public housing under the rule. They must also provide a Social Security number, which wasn't previously required of every resident. By Dec. 14, tenants need to provide evidence to landlords that they are eligible to remain in their housing. By Jan. 11, if tenants haven't submitted that documentation, public housing authorities and landlords receiving federal subsidy must begin notifying those tenants that they have to provide documentation or vacate the property. If the tenant fails to prove their eligibility, under the updated rule, their rental assistance must be terminated. The rule is an enormous undertaking for public housing authorities, especially in such a short span of time, said La Shelle Dozier, CEO of the industry group the Council of Large Public Housing Authorities . “There's a huge regulatory burden in terms of administering the program, and now you're adding on another layer of complexity,” she said, adding that staff will also need to be trained to help landlords comply. “There just isn't enough time.” Housing providers voiced their opposition to the rule during its public comment period earlier this year. HUD received more than 16,000 comments on the rule, including from more than 100 housing authorities, financing agencies, apartment associations and landlords. “Destabilizing thousands of households will not expand housing opportunity,” the California Association of Housing Authorities, which represents 91 public housing authorities, said in its public comment . “It will intensify displacement pressure in an already strained system.” The rule creates broad changes in who’s eligible to live in HUD-subsidized housing, potentially resulting in dramatic changes in occupancy, advocates said. Wikimedia Commons/The White House The changes to rules around eligibility for federally subsidized housing will stop individuals from "exploiting government-funded welfare programs," HUD Secretary Scott Turner said. Previously, HUD allowed mixed-status households, where only some residents have documentation, to receive federal assistance. Those households are eligible for prorated assistance, where residents with documents proving their immigration status receive subsidies and residents who can’t prove their eligibility pay full rent. Without that assistance, families will be forced to choose either to ask some members of their households to move out or to leave their homes altogether and try to find units on the open market and risk living in unsafe housing or on the street, Tran-Leung said. “HUD is trying to enlist housing providers in its immigration enforcement,” Tran-Leung said. “That is something that I think makes a lot of them feel deeply uncomfortable and very outside of the scope of their mission of providing affordable housing .” Because mixed-status families receive less subsidy and pay more rent, removing them from federally funded housing means that building owners will get less cash for repairs and maintenance, Tran-Leung said. “One of the things that HUD actually acknowledged in its regulatory impact analysis of the proposed rule was that if these families are forced to leave, there will be less funding available for HUD-assisted housing,” she said. “That reduces the housing supply and worsens the housing crisis for everyone.” The rule will also impact tenants who are eligible but may not have the required documents, Dozier said. items.title: Data Center Developer, South Jersey University Team Up To Address Sector's Labor Shortage
items.description: The level of data center development in the U.S. is outpacing the number of workers who know how to run the facilities, so one developer and operator of a large-scale South Jersey project has turned to a local university to help bolster the region's pipeline of skilled talent. Courtesy of DataOne A rendering of DataOne's upcoming Vineland project DataOne is bringing in Rowan University engineering students for a full-time co-op at the firm’s upcoming facility in Vineland. The 718K SF data center is planned to have 350 megawatts of capacity and employ 200 full-time workers. The program will start with four participants, but DataOne CEO Charles-Antoine Beyney eventually aims to double or triple that number. “This is a way for us to be sure we’re always going to have a pool of talent,” he said. “It’s training the next generation. We need people who know how to operate these facilities,” the executive added. “That kills two birds with the same stone.” More than half of data center operators said they were struggling to fill open positions in the first half of this year, according to a July report from industry think tank Uptime Institute . Turnover has become a problem as the labor shortage leads operators to lure qualified workers away from each other. The DataOne program’s competitive application process will begin after the company gives a presentation next month to prospective participants on Rowan’s main campus, about 20 miles north of the data center. It will pick two electrical engineering students and two mechanical engineering students who will commute to the site daily for between eight and 10 months next year for credit instead of attending classes. The facility isn’t set to be fully delivered until 2028, so Beyney said this first cohort of students will assist with the construction process. DataOne has a longstanding relationship with the public university and has given presentations there before. “Our engineering students learn best when they can put what they study in the classroom to work in the real world,” Rowan Chancellor Tony Lowman said in a statement. “Partnerships like this one, with companies willing to open their doors, train our students and invest in their growth, are essential.” Like many data centers, the facility in Vineland has fielded intense pushback from many in the community. Much of it is tied to concerns about noise and emissions from the natural gas plant that DataOne is building on the site. “It’s hard to grasp the size of this thing. It is staggering,” South Jersey resident and former political candidate Bayly Winder told Bisnow in April after he participated in the protests. “If it sounds like the Turnpike next to your window because of a data center, that’s a problem,” he added. Beyney was proud of the project’s massive scale and said the community tensions didn’t lead to any friction with Rowan when it came to setting up the co-op. “The good thing is when you’re talking to universities, they’re not big on biased information,” he said of the school’s administrators, some of whom have visited the site. “They know what’s going on,” Beyney added. “They understood it was real tangible jobs with real expertise.” Vineland is a relatively low-income community. Its poverty rate sat at 14.6% last year, which was higher than the 8.7% across New Jersey as a whole, according to the U.S. Census Bureau . Beyney said this was attractive because he wants DataOne’s economic development potential — which already includes 100 full-time positions at manufacturing facilities and 500 construction jobs — to uplift places that need it the most. “It was very important for me to be in a local underprivileged community,” he said. “You’re going to one of the poorest neighborhoods in South Jersey,” Beyney added. “All the jobs and taxes you’re paying will make a big difference.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: Bayly Winder , Charles-Antoine Beyney , DataOne , Rowan University , Tony Lowman , Uptime Institute

items.title: Gaylord Rockies To Undergo $305M Expansion: The Denver Deal Sheet
items.description: Wikimedia Commons/Cswat Gaylord Rockies Hotel In Aurora, Colorado Gaylord Rockies Resort & Convention Center in Aurora will undergo a massive expansion, making it the third-largest Gaylord Hotels property by room count. The $305M expansion will add 450 guest rooms, a 110K SF “luxury indoor water experience” and a multilevel parking garage to the property at 6700 N. Gaylord Rockies Blvd., according to a statement from owner Ryman Hospitality Properties . The water park addition will include seven rides, a wave pool, a river, a kids’ area, a 144-seat restaurant and more, according to the statement. The expansion comes as group demand has continued to exceed the hotel’s available room supply, said Ryman Hospitality Properties CEO and President Mark Fioravanti. The hotel turned down 38% of large-group room nights from 2023 to 2025 due to capacity constraints, he said. Preconstruction work will begin in December. The new rooms are expected to be delivered in the first quarter of 2029, with work on the indoor water park finishing in late 2029. The project is expected to be funded with cash on hand and borrowings under Ryman Hospitality Properties’ credit facility. The Weitz Co. will serve as the general contractor. PEOPLE Tim and Jack Richey and Cartter Berg joined Cushman & Wakefield to form an institutional capital markets team in Denver. Tim Richey is rejoining Cushman & Wakefield as executive vice chair after serving as executive vice chairman of Newmark’s Capital Markets division in Denver. With more than 16 years of experience, Cartter joins Cushman & Wakefield as executive managing director. Jack Richey, formerly at Newmark, joins as a director. SALES An entity tied to Colorado Springs-based Venu Holdings Corp. closed on a sale-leaseback for its yet-to-open music venue and restaurant in Centennial . Venu sold the land at the northwest corner of Parker and Arapahoe roads to The Haven LLC for $7.5M. The Haven will lease the property to Venu for at least 25 years with a base rent of $600K each year. The agreement also includes an option for Venu to repurchase the land by 2033 for $8.5M, according to a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. The $75M venue and restaurant , called Bourbon Brothers Smokehouse & Tavern and The Hall at Bourbon Brothers, is expected to open in mid-2027. LEASES Aerospace company Leap signed a 75,600 SF lease for a manufacturing facility at 11210 Wadsworth Parkway in Broomfield. The company expects to move into the space, which will also serve as its headquarters, by March 2027. Leap has more than 50 employees in Colorado but expects to have 130 by the end of 2027. Leap is the first tenant to sign at the larger 360K SF industrial development in Broomfield, called Arista 36. The company signed a 10.5-year lease. *** California-based Fivetran opened its new 33K SF space at Steel House in Denver’s River North Art District. The 12th-floor office space at 3100 Brighton Blvd. will support the software company’s approximately 200 Denver employees. Fivetran was the first company to sign a lease at the development , which was delivered in 2025. *** Westbound & Down Brewing Co. opened an approximately 2,300 SF taproom in Longmont at 142 Pratt St. The new location also features a 775 SF patio and allows the brewery to increase its production capacity. Westbound & Down has brewpubs in Denver, Lafayette and Idaho Springs. *** BodySpec opened its first Colorado brick-and-mortar in Cherry Creek at 250 Steele St., Suite 350. The 2,600 SF space will be used for medical-grade body scans that provide customers with data about their lean muscle mass, bone density and body fat. CONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT Courtesy of Playground Garages Playground Garages of Centennial will feature 62 for-sale garage condominiums. Littleton developer Playground Garages is expanding to Centennial with a 72K SF for-sale garage condominium project east of Denver Summit FC’s temporary stadium. The development at 7020 S. Kenton St. will feature 62 customizable garages geared toward automotive enthusiasts, entrepreneurs and business owners and a shared 1,400 SF owner’s suite. The project broke ground on Nov. 19 and is expected to deliver in late fall 2027. California-based Talonvest Capital provided nearly $4.8M toward the project through a joint venture with Clark Investment Group. FINANCING Kairoi Residential secured a nearly $88.3M bridge financing loan for The Vixen, a multifamily building at 1150 E. Colfax Ave. JLL worked with Kairoi to secure the loan through a “global alternative asset manager,” JLL said in a statement. Construction on The Vixen wrapped up in 2025. The seven-story building offers 334 units and a surplus of amenities. THIS AND THAT Wikimedia Commons/Xnatedawgx A study by the Urban Land Institute and funded by the Denver Downtown Development Authority recommends “transforming” the majority of the Denver Pavilions into a “culturally significant, free, continuously programmed open space.” This would include demolishing most of the commercial district but keeping the building that houses the movie theater and redeveloping the two city blocks. ULI estimates demolition and construction would cost between $498M and $615M. The Pavilions will not be demolished unless it’s in conjunction with redevelopment, according to the study. Next, DDA will put together a committee to evaluate ULI’s recommendations and help determine a path forward for the Pavilions. DDA purchased the Pavilions, an underground parking garage and two adjacent parking lots, for $37M last December . It has invested more than $3M in capital improvements since May. items.title: Some FHA borrowers pay mortgage insurance for a decade or more. There's an industry push to change the rules
items.description: Read more CNBC personal finance coverage How to get Anthropic stock — without buying the IPO There's a growing 'property tax revolt' as homeowners face rising costs Congress passes bill to protect older investors from financial fraud CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 The push, which revives a longstanding mortgage industry request, also comes several weeks after President Donald Trump issued an executive order that included calling for the launch of a federal pilot program that would cancel mortgage insurance on certain conventional loans once borrowers meet equity requirements. The order would apply generally to future loans backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac — two government-sponsored enterprises that purchase qualifying mortgages from lenders and resell them as bundled securities. It wouldn't apply to FHA loans. Here's who uses FHA mortgages FHA mortgages are issued by private lenders but insured by the federal government, which protects lenders against losses if a borrower defaults. The loans are designed to make homeownership more accessible, particularly for borrowers with limited savings for a down payment or with lower credit scores. Affordability challenges persist in the housing market, with elevated home prices and mortgage rates putting homeownership out of reach for many prospective buyers. Existing homeowners are also facing rising costs alongside their mortgages, including property taxes and homeowners insurance amid overall high inflation . About 83% of new FHA purchase loans went to first-time homebuyers in the most recent fiscal year, according to the FHA report to Congress. Altogether, the FHA insured more than 8.4 million mortgages as of Sept. 30. The median age of first-time buyers is 40, according to a new report from the National Association of Realtors. watch now VIDEO 0:31 00:31 Can you afford to buy a home? Personal Finance FHA loans also require borrowers to pay mortgage insurance regardless of the size of their down payment. Under current rules established in 2013 , FHA borrowers with a down payment that's less than 10% of the loan must pay mortgage insurance premiums for the duration of the loan. Those who put 10% or more down pay that insurance for 11 years. Borrowers generally pay both an upfront mortgage insurance premium and an annual premium, which is typically divided into monthly payments. The upfront premium is usually 1.75% of the base loan amount and can be financed into the mortgage. For many borrowers with 30-year FHA loans, the annual premium is 0.55% of the outstanding loan balance. Conventional mortgages generally don't require mortgage insurance unless the loan is for more than 80% of the home's value. In 2022, the premium typically ranged from 0.58% to 1.86% annually, according to Fannie Mae . If those borrowers have to pay mortgage insurance, they can typically request its removal once they've built 20% equity in the home, or it is automatically canceled when their loan drops to 78% of the original value. Proposals from the mortgage industry The mortgage industry has floated two different proposals. One would reduce the rate that applies to FHA mortgage insurance. For example, the Mortgage Bankers Association recently suggested a rate reduction of 20 basis points , which would lower the standard 0.55% rate to 0.35% for new borrowers. For example: On a $350,000 mortgage, a 0.55% rate generally translates into $1,925 annually, or about $160 monthly, at the start of the loan. As the principal owed slowly goes down over time through a borrower's monthly payments, so does that mortgage insurance amount. At 0.35%, the annual premium would be $1,225 at the start of the loan, or $102 monthly — a difference of $58 per month. The FHA last cut that rate in 2023 , when it was reduced from 0.85%. At the time, HUD estimated that affected borrowers would save an average of $800 annually. However, in the FHA's new report to Congress, the agency noted that the 2023 cut has reduced the fund's revenue, contributing to a decline in its capital ratio. The other industry proposal would implement auto-cancellation of premiums once the loan balance fell to 78% of the home's original value at purchase — in other words, the same as for Fannie- and Freddie-backed mortgages. Cancellation prevents the squeeze for borrowers who have paid down their loans and shouldn't be paying for coverage they have outgrown. Michael Farrell National Association of Mortgage Brokers "Cancellation prevents the squeeze for borrowers who have paid down their loans and shouldn't be paying for coverage they have outgrown," said Michael Farrell, president of the National Association of Mortgage Brokers, a trade group that generally has supported the cancellation proposal. "NAMB believes that cancellation at 78% protects the [FHA insurance fund], because premiums can restart if the [capital] ratio ever falls to 2%," Farrell said. FHA mortgages received that treatment from 2001 through 2013, but the agency eliminated it to shore up its insurance fund after financial reserves deteriorated over time following the housing market crash, which led to the 2008 financial crisis. Whether the proposals will go anywhere this time is uncertain. HUD, which oversees the FHA, did not respond to a CNBC email seeking more information. items.title: President Woodrow Wilson’s Historic Princeton Home Lists for $5.85 Million After a 7-Year Restoration
items.description: The home where Woodrow Wilson lives as a professor before becoming president has hit the market in Princeton, NJ for $5.85 million. The Tudor Revival at 82 Library Place was built in 1896 for Wilson and he lived there with his wife, Ellen, and their three children until 1902, when he became president of Princeton University and moved on campus. The home was first listed in May 2025 for $6.5 million. “Wilson and his wife had a lot of input in the design and finishes chosen for the home, which included double stained-glass doors from the Sears catalog,” says listing agent Barbara Blackwell of Callaway Henderson Sotheby’s International Realty . Loading... The backyard comes with garden-lined patios and a koi pond Callaway Henderson Sotheby’s International Realty Loading... The home underwent a seven year top-to-bottom restoration Callaway Henderson Sotheby’s International Realty Loading... Inside the new sunroom Callaway Henderson Sotheby’s International Realty The estate is one of only two working homes in the U.S. designed and built by a president, the other being Monticello, according to the listing. Blackwell says the house has had 19 owners since the Wilsons, including Princeton University itself, which used the home as faculty housing during the Great Depression. The current owners spent seven years restoring the property with architect Ron Berlin and Baxter Construction. The award-winning project brought back the original beams and woodwork and re-glassed the leaded windows. It also gave the home a distinct sense of presidential charm, making it easy to imagine Wilson tucked among its interiors. The work also restored the stucco and timber exterior, added a cedar shake roof and a generator, and updated all mechanical systems. The three-story home includes seven bedrooms and 5.5 bathrooms. Wilson once taught students in the spacious foyer, which opens to a wood-paneled library the current owners added. Stained-glass pocket doors lead to a dining room with a commissioned mural of campus landmarks. Loading... The current owners also added this wood-paneled library Callaway Henderson Sotheby’s International Realty Loading... A light-filled third floor space Callaway Henderson Sotheby’s International Realty Loading... The dining room comes with a custom mural depicting university landmarks Callaway Henderson Sotheby’s International Realty The kitchen pairs restored original cabinetry with new matching pieces. It also has a copper drainboard sink, a working dumbwaiter, and a double Wolf range. Nearby, a new glass-roofed sunroom with a wet bar overlooks the grounds. “The sunroom is a perfect blends interior and exterior with views of the gardens and flowering trees,” Blackwell says. Of the four bedrooms on the second floor, one is a soundproofed primary suite with a coffee bar and a radiant-heated marble bathroom that opens onto a balcony. The skylit third floor contains three more bedrooms, a bathroom, laundry and a cedar walk-in closet. Outside, the recently redesigned gardens surround two patios, a fountain and a koi pond. The 0.74-acre lot also has a circular driveway lined with boxwoods, an office in a former porte cochere and a restored, oversized two-car garage in the same Tudor style as the house. The property is in Princeton’s Western Section and backs up to the current home of the university’s president. Nassau Street’s shops and restaurants are a short walk away. “This home represents a substantial piece of history with all the modern conveniences of a new home,” Blackwell says. The owner’s collection of Wilson books and memorabilia can be bought separately. items.description: A 25-foot-wide townhouse with a carriage house has just hit the market for $11.95 million in Manhattan’s Carnegie Hill . items.title: Inside a Secluded Cabin Hidden Right Beneath Big Sur’s Iconic Landmark
items.description: A secluded retreat tucked beneath one of California ’s most photographed landmarks in Big Sur has come on the market for $3.65 million. The home at 39320 Coast Road sits in Bixby Canyon and is one of only seven residences behind a private gate. “Millions recognize Bixby Bridge, yet very few will ever experience the landscape beneath it,” says listing agent Michael Hornig of the Strock Team at eXp Realty . Loading... The entrance of the cabin, which is one of only seven properties in the canyon. Lost Coast Media Loading... The main room and kitchen Lost Coast Media Loading... A cozy living room Lost Coast Media The canyon also comes with a literary history: In 1960, Jack Kerouac retreated to a cabin here owned by Lawrence Ferlinghetti , the poet and co-founder of City Lights Bookstore. His time in the canyon formed the basis for his 1962 novel, “Big Sur.” While this is not the original Kerouac cabin, it shares the same setting. According to Hornig, the canyon has also been home to the film director Sam Peckinpah and the Disney illustrator Ron Dias. “There’s an extraordinary feeling about this canyon,” Hornig says. “You’re surrounded by a landscape that inspired some of America’s most influential writers, and remarkably, much of that atmosphere of solitude and wilderness remains intact today.” Built in 1984, the single-level home has three bedrooms, two full bathrooms, and 1,489 square feet of living space. Vaulted, open-beam ceilings, hardwood floors, and three wood-burning stoves characterize the interiors, as do large windows that frame the surrounding redwoods. A wraparound porch overlooks the forest. “Luxury doesn’t always have to be expressed through scale or elaborate architecture,” Hornig says. “Here, the luxury is the relationship between the home and its surroundings.” Loading... One of three bedrooms Lost Coast Media Loading... A soaking tub under the redwoods Lost Coast Media Loading... A wraparound deck with canyon views Lost Coast Media The property covers two parcels: a 0.79-acre residential lot and an adjacent 0.33-acre creekside lot. It is move-in ready, with a private well, septic system, and electricity. There is also a fenced backyard, storage shed, pasture space and parking for 10 vehicles, including EV charging. Owners share access to a privately held canyon enclave of more than 140 acres. There, a creekside trail winds through redwoods and ferns to a secluded beach beneath the bridge. “You can walk from your front door through a redwood forest, follow the creek toward the Pacific, and emerge beneath one of the most recognizable bridges in the world,” Hornig says. Next to the property, Brazil Ranch adds about 1,200 acres of U.S. Forest Service land for hiking, hunting, and recreation. The historic Old Coast Road offers miles of biking, horseback riding, and backcountry exploration. Highway 1 is about five minutes away. Carmel, Monterey, and Big Sur’s restaurants and state parks are about 20 minutes away. “To me, the greatest luxury here is the privilege of belonging to a landscape that most people will only ever admire from a distance,” Hornig says. "It's this contrast between one of California’s most recognizable landmarks and the hidden residential community beneath it." items.title: Texas Housing Insight | November 2026 | Texas Real Estate Research Center
items.description: Texas Housing Insight | November 2026 Texas’ housing market continued to soften in September as rising mortgage rates, inflation, and affordability challenges restrained buyer demand, slowed sales, and kept home-price growth muted. By Yanling Mayer quick links September continued to see a pullback in market momentum, as seasonal cooling combined with rising mortgage rates, rising inflationary pressures, and affordability constraints dampened buyer activity. Existing-home sales declined from a year earlier, and market activity remained subdued. Fewer than two out of every ten homes listed for sale during the month were sold (1.5 homes), highlighting slower inventory turnover and longer marketing times amid challenging demand conditions. Year to date, sales remain modestly ahead of last year’s pace, suggesting housing demand has not deteriorated from last year. Home-price growth remained muted. Statewide home prices were essentially unchanged from a year ago, as gains in a handful of markets were offset by continued weakness elsewhere. Major metropolitan areas, including Austin, Dallas, and San Antonio, continued to experience measurable downward price pressure, while Houston and the Fort Worth metro division showed signs of modest stabilization. On the supply side, inventory levels eased seasonally following their summer peak, consistent with typical market patterns heading into the fall and winter. Nevertheless, overall inventory remains only slightly below peak summer levels, indicating that the inventory condition remains favorable to buyers. Looking ahead, the housing market is expected to remain soft through the remainder of the year. Mortgage rates are near current multi-decade highs, limiting purchasing power and sidelining prospective buyers. Unless financing conditions improve meaningfully, housing demand is likely to remain restrained, resulting in slower sales and weak prices. Disclaimer: The September 2026 figures are based on more complete data and have been revised from their initial release. Year-Over-Year Sales Down Table 1: September 2026 State & National Sales Notes: The sales numbers reflect actual sales, not the seasonally adjusted rate. Source: Texas REALTORS® and National Association of REALTORS® and U.S. Census Bureau data In September, Texas recorded 20,200 existing-home sales statewide, down 1.6 percent year over year (YoY). September marked a second consecutive month of YoY sales declines. As of 3Q2026, year-to-date (YTD) sales volume rose 3.3 percent from last year. As of September, median existing-home price was $325,000, softening slightly from August’s $330,000 and unchanged from a year ago. Nationally, seasonally unadjusted existing home sales were down 3.9 percent YoY, a second consecutive month of sales declines, while YTD sales volumes remained slightly ahead of last year’s pace. National median price reached $422,700, maintaining a steady growth pace at about 1.4 percent YoY. September’s new-home sales in U.S. declined 3.4 percent YoY. As of the third quarter, YTD new-home sales were 2.9 percent below last year’s pace. Monthly Market Snapshot: September Sales and Inventory Trends Table 2: Texas Housing Market Indicators Notes: The turnover rate is calculated as pending sales divided by inventory, where inventory is the average of month-beginning and month-ending inventory Source: Texas Real Estate Research Center analysis of Data Relevance Project and Texas REALTORS® data Homes sold in September spent an average of 65 days on the market (DoM), compared to a similar 63 days a year ago. Inventory turnover was slow at 15 percent, down from 16.2 percent a year ago. At this pace, fewer than two in ten existing homes (1.5 homes) on the market went under contract during the month. The median seller price cut remained similar to a year ago at $15,000, equivalent to roughly 4.5 percent of the initial listing price. As of September, active inventory is at a 5.7-month supply, similar to a year ago. The unsold inventory has an average DoM of 98 days, compared to a DoM of 65 days among the sold. New Listing Activity Eases Seasonally, Remaining Near Year-Ago Levels Figure 1: Monthly New-Listing Activity, 2026 Source : Texas Real Estate Research Center analysis of Data Relevance Project, Texas REALTORS® data Statewide, 47,580 new listings were recorded, down 2.1 percent from August, reflecting the typical seasonal slowdown as the market moves into the fall and winter months. September’s new listings remained 2.1 percent above September 2025 levels. Through September, year-to-date listing activity was largely unchanged from last year, edging down just 0.3 percent. Among the major metros, YoY new-listing activity increased 7.7 percent in Austin, 3 percent in Houston, and 3.8 percent in San Antonio, while DFW posted a 2.0 decline, continuing a stretch of relatively weak new-listing activity that began in April (see Table 4). The YTD activity in Austin, Houston, and San Antonio all remained slightly ahead of last year’s pace; in DFW it trailed by 3.2 percent. Inventory Levels Slightly Below the Summer Peak Figure 2: Monthly Active Inventory, 2026 Source : Texas Real Estate Research Center analysis of Data Relevance Project, Texas REALTORS® data At the end of September, the for-sale inventory stood at nearly 154,200 listings, up 5.6 percent from a year earlier. Although inventory continued its seasonal easing, September levels remained only slightly below the peak reached in July. Inventory trends varied across the major metropolitan areas (see Table 4). YoY inventory increased 3.9 percent in Austin, 7.3 percent in Houston, and 1.6 percent in San Antonio, while DFW recorded a 6 percent decline. Houston remained the only major metro where inventory levels have largely held near their summer peak since July. Other markets experienced more noticeable seasonal declines. items.description: Federal Reserve announces College Fed Challenge winners For release at 4:15 p.m. EST Share --> --> --> --> --> --> The University of California, Los Angeles won the 23rd Annual National College Fed Challenge. ' data-gallery='global-photo' data-toggle="lightbox"> The University of California, Los Angeles won the 23rd Annual National College Fed Challenge. The University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) won the 23rd annual national College Fed Challenge on Friday, a team competition that encourages undergraduate students to learn about the U.S. economy, monetary policymaking, and the role of the Federal Reserve System. Teams analyze economic and financial conditions and formulate a monetary policy recommendation, modeling the Federal Open Market Committee. The team, from Los Angeles, California, represented the San Francisco District and included Aarushi Maheshwari, Annika Chan, Atul Prasanth, Caitlyn Cox, Finn Karish, Eli Brooks (alternate), Kennedy Yang (alternate), Manasi Vartak (alternate), Ronojoy Borpujari (alternate), and Sahil Sudani (alternate). The team's advisers were Chris Surro and Ali Haider Ismail. "I am very happy to congratulate the students who competed in this year's College Fed Challenge, especially the winners and finalists," said Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh. "They took on the same big questions we policymakers face. I'm impressed by their talent, their rigor, and their eagerness to think hard about monetary policy and the economy." This year's College Fed Challenge included 141 schools from 34 states across the nation, the most in the competition's history. Teams submitted video presentations or participated in local competitions last month. Twenty-one semi-finalist teams then participated in question-and-answer sessions held earlier this month, and seven finalists were invited to the Federal Reserve Board for the national finals. The other national finalists were the University of Chicago in second place and the University of Maryland, College Park in third place. Teams with honorable mentions include Cleveland State University, Harvard College, Pennsylvania State University, and St. Lawrence University. Teams were evaluated on their economic analysis, responses to the judges' questions, teamwork, and presentations. For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call 202-452-2955. items.title: Beyond the Rent: In an era of tech outages, here’s how apartment firms can prepare their networks
items.description: Beyond the Rent: In an era of tech outages, here’s how apartment firms can prepare their networks Former CISA Director Chris Krebs told OPTECH attendees that they need to know which AI tools employees and vendors are using. Published Nov. 20, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Chris Krebs speaks at OPTECH 2026 on Nov. 17. Les Shaver/Multifamily Dive Beyond the Rent is Multifamily Dive’s analysis of the trends driving supply, demand and operations in the apartment industry. You can read the previous edition here . The Real Estate Technology & Transformation Center picked a helluva time to hold OPTECH 2026, which ran from Nov. 16 to 18 at the MGM Grand Hotel & Casino in Las Vegas. In the week before the conference began, a Microsoft 365 outage disrupted Outlook , angering users worldwide (including this one). The next day, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop, while Workday also had a much less high-profile outage that day. For people like me who don’t like getting on planes (it’s not about crashing; it's about not having control, as I often tell my wife), the ground stop was alarming. The week of OPTECH, outages followed at JPMorgan Chase, Apple, the National Security Agency and, to my chagrin, briefly, United. That one led to a minor freakout as I walked the OPTECH expo floor. My apologies to those of you who chose to speak with me. In an extremely fortunate bit of planning, RETTC actually booked former United States Director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency Chris Krebs to speak on Tuesday. It wasn’t surprising to learn that he tore up his original presentation to focus on current events. With the FAA having a hardware-related shutdown, Krebs’ explanation for the majority of the disruptions was that artificial intelligence is helping firms find software flaws. As they scramble to patch issues, outages occur. “We're going to have more outages,” Krebs said. “But I also think we're going to learn from every one of these. So there are always lessons learned, whether it's from the Chase, United [and] from Microsoft.” However, he emphasized this won’t be a short-term process. “The good news is we're almost done, right?” Krebs said. “Nope. We're in like the second inning of this ball game.” How apartment firms can fortify their systems For apartment firms looking to protect their own systems, Krebs said the first place to start is by peeking under the hood and seeing what’s happening in their own companies. Find out what AI tools employees are using. “You have a pretty significant risk at that point of a PII [personally identifiable information] or other sensitive data leak,” Krebs said. “So you've got to be very cognizant of any sort of AI use in your environment, what it touches, including the secrets, the keys that it has access to. That can get out, and then you've got a completely different problem with a data breach.” Apartment firms also need to know who inside the organization owns the problem if something goes wrong and where the kill switch is. If “it's either misbehaving or the vendor is a jerk, and I want to turn it off, how do I do that?” Krebs said. Suppliers also deserve scrutiny, according to Krebs. “You're going to have to extend that review and analysis to your vendors because every one of your vendors is probably using AI, and I'm not quite sure if they're telling you,” he said. “So, vendors in the room, be transparent.” Above all, companies that develop their own products need to know their exposure and quickly patch any issues, which is reportedly happening across the broader economy right now. “If you do develop code, and a lot of you do for some of your proprietary products, make sure that you're using AI to scan the code that's being developed,” Krebs said. “Now, don't just grab some random open source model. There are specific harnesses and products that are developed specifically for secure coding.” Krebs’ points struck a chord with me. In the midst of the chaos, it may be a good time for apartment executives to look at their own systems and determine what happens if there’s an outage. While I can’t control United’s schedule from the OPTECH exhibition floor (in case you’re wondering, I made my flight and am writing this final paragraph from the friendly skies above Champaign, Illinois), multifamily leaders can prepare for what’s coming. items.title: The 10 states set to build the least housing in the coming years – Business Insider
items.description: Some states across America need to pick up the homebuilding pace — or housing prices could catch up to them. From January to August 2026, the US national average for housing permits — indicating how many housing units are approved to be built — was 2.83 units per 1,000 residents, according to an October research report from the Lied Center for Real Estate at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. The report provides insights into what the housing market could look like in 2028 and 2029, as these approved permits come online as available housing units, said Nicholas Irwin, coauthor of the report and research director at the Lied Center for Real Estate. Across the country, some states lag behind the national average, which could drive up housing prices in the near future as housing supply fails to catch up with demand. "If you don't add supply, and demand keeps growing as more people move in and more households are formed, it just puts upward pressure on prices," Irwin said. Here are the states that are issuing permits at the lowest rate per 1,000 residents. The states lagging in issuing building permits could face growing affordability concerns, especially those falling short of projected household growth, another measure included in the report. "If we are already at a lag in some of these states — your Nevadas, your Connecticut's, Maryland's — when it comes to building, that's just going to exacerbate currently experienced affordability concerns for each of those states' residents," Irwin said. Alaska was the state with the lowest ranking, standing at 0.72 permits per 1,000 residents, after only 528 units were approved from January through August 2026, 75% below the national rate, the report said. Its permit acceptances have also declined year-over-year, down 8.3% from the same period in 2025 and 12.3% from 2023. Connecticut was ranked the second-lowest state in number of permits per resident in the US, as it approved 3,799 permits, 64% below the national rate. This rate is 17.7% less than during January to August of 2025, and 9.3% lower than the same period in 2023. It was the lowest-ranked state in the report's overall housing supply pipeline rankings — performing poorly across four metrics, including the permit rate per 1,000 residents. Regarding the overall ranking, Irwin said some states are struggling on all fronts. "Nevada, Alaska, Connecticut, North Dakota, Maryland are all doing really poorly, and they're doing poorly no matter how much we weigh our different four pillars," Irwin said. West Virginia was ranked the 10th-lowest state in building permits per resident, at 1.55, 45% below the US average. Overall, it ranked 22nd in the report, with mixed performance across metrics. While its overall number of permits per resident lagged behind other states, its pace of permits relative to household growth was the third-highest in the nation — meaning permitting is outpacing its projected household growth by 5.72. This is because the number of households is projected to shrink in West Virginia, according to the report. Irwin said there are some states that "no matter how you weigh" them consistently end up at the top or bottom of the rankings. "No matter how you look at the data, the building permit regime and how housing is being constructed in these areas is falling way behind of what's needed," he said. "Our main thing, if we can give anything, is just build more housing, build all types of housing."

items.title: Everyday Economics: The federal government delayed the housing recovery – The Center Square
items.description: Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Houses line a suburban neighborhood. Photo: Alan Wooten / The Center Square Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save (The Center Square) – Existing-home sales fell in October to their slowest pace since August 2010, according to the National Association of Realtors . Federal policy is pulling in two directions: HUD has cut lenders’ costs on taxpayer-backed FHA loans, while tariffs, the conflict with Iran and federal borrowing add to the inflation and interest-rate pressures that keep mortgages expensive. According to Freddie Mac , the 30-year fixed rate has been climbing since the war began and now exceeds year ago levels. According to the National Association of Realtors , October existing-home sales fell to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million, the weakest pace since August 2010, and 8.8% below a year earlier. According to my calculations using NAR’s unadjusted data , actual October closings fell 11.7%, partly because October had one fewer business day than last year. The unadjusted annual decline deepened sharply from September’s 4.2%. The year started better than those figures suggest. According to the same calculations, 3.4 million homes sold through October, just 0.6% fewer than during the same period in 2025. My October housing report , based on Redfin data, found that seasonally adjusted pending sales fell 3.6% from September to their lowest level since April 2020. The same report found that active listings increased even though fewer sellers listed, because homes are selling more slowly. The problem is still affordability. My report calculated that monthly principal and interest on the median-priced home reached $2,137 with 20% down, up 11.2% from a year earlier. By my calculation, higher rates added approximately $223 to the monthly payment, while a slightly lower Redfin median sale price saved about $7. HUD has targeted a different cost: making the loan. According to HUD , June changes streamlined FHA appraisal-review requirements and eliminated a duplicative homebuyer disclosure form. HUD estimates the appraisal change alone saves lenders about $425 per review, or roughly $3.3 million a year industrywide. HUD’s announcement does not say how much of those savings will reach borrowers. The Appraisal Institute has said eliminating long-standing review requirements raises questions about oversight of collateral on FHA loans, which the federal government insures, American Banker reported . Any savings from lower origination costs are expected to be small next to the roughly $223 a month that higher rates added to the typical payment. Other federal policies affect what borrowers pay each month. According to Federal Reserve Bank of New York researchers , tariffs raise prices for imported and domestically produced goods. According to the Energy Information Administration , attacks on tankers, constrained shipping and falling inventories pushed oil prices higher again in October. Federal borrowing matters, too. According to the Congressional Budget Office , growing government debt crowds out private investment and contributes to higher interest rates. My analysis found that sticky inflation and worries about U.S. fiscal sustainability have pushed long-term Treasury yields higher, and mortgage rates track those long-term yields far more closely than the Federal Reserve’s policy rate. Producer prices are still rising. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), producer prices rose 6.5% over the year through October, their largest increase since November 2022. BLS reported that truck freight prices rose 3.9% in October, accounting for more than 80% of the increase in services prices, even as diesel prices fell 7.9% from September. Truck freight prices were up 24.6% from a year earlier, according to BLS. According to my analysis of BLS producer price data, retail margins narrowed for computers, appliances and sporting goods, consistent with shoppers resisting higher prices. This week’s retail sales report could help clarify how spending is holding up. Retail sales and builder confidence arrive Tuesday, followed by housing starts and permits Wednesday. He has briefed the White House Council of Economic Advisers, testified before state legislatures, and delivers more than 30 speaking engagements annually.
