items.title: How Much of a Pay Raise Would Today’s Renters Need to Afford a Home? – MortgagePoint
items.description: How Much of a Pay Raise Would Today's Renters Need to Afford a Home? Demetria C. Lester November 13, 2026 Seeking a more suburban lifestyle—with the additional space, yard, and private garage often found in a single-family home—does not necessarily require stretching the budget to buy. For most families, buying is a significant financial stretch. A household that can comfortably afford rent on a single-family home would need a $14,408 pay increase to cover the monthly costs of owning one, even before setting aside money for a down payment. Across the country, the typical rent for a single-family home is $2,243 per month, compared with $2,603 per month to own one with a 20% down payment—a difference of $360 each month. Using the common guideline of spending no more than 30% of household income on housing, a household needs to earn $89,724 to comfortably afford rent and $104,132 to buy. For many households, renting a house is a deliberate choice, not a fallback. It requires less income than ownership and leaves more room in the monthly budget. The income increase required to buy a home is now the largest since early 2025, exceeding twice the $6,463 needed in February 2026, when mortgage rates briefly dipped below 6%. The difference varies considerably by market. It is greatest in San Jose, where the income needed to buy ($404,925) is more than twice the income needed to rent ($190,561)—a gap of $214,364. San Francisco has the next-largest gap at $139,353, followed by San Diego ($84,101), New York ($78,208) and Los Angeles ($78,003). The smallest annual differences are in Pittsburgh ($2,554), Houston ($4,500) and Cincinnati ($4,774). Buffalo is the only market where buying would not require an income increase. Even after securing that increase, prospective buyers face another challenge: saving for a 20% down payment. According to Zillow’s 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report, about 30% of mortgage buyers receive a gift or loan from family or friends, while 46% rely on at least two sources, including down payment assistance programs. Beyond monthly expenses, households weighing renting against buying should consider purchase-related upfront costs, the potential to build equity and renters’ option to invest the money they would otherwise use for a down payment. Zillow’s rent-versus-buy analysis estimates the national break-even point—the time an owner must stay in a home for buying to become more advantageous than renting—at 7.8 years with a 20% down payment. As renting a house becomes an increasingly attractive value, more people are choosing to rent. Nationwide rental demand has risen 22.1% year over year, according to the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index (ZORDI). Demand for single-family rentals is up 24.3%, about twice the 12.1% increase for multifamily rentals. Demand increased most in San Jose, where ZORDI is 78.9% higher than a year ago. San Francisco followed at 60.5%, then Austin at 59.6%, Miami at 51.5% and Jacksonville at 47.9%. Absorption was strongest in the northern suburbs and core neighborhoods, led by Allen/McKinney, Frisco, and Intown Dallas. Dallas held steady at about 30%. The northern decline reflects fewer sales of newer properties, which drove much of that area's 2025 activity, as loan assumptions and value-add purchases also slowed. items.title: New Home Market Update
items.description: New Home Market Update Zonda tracks 85% of the production new home market across the United States. Given the proprietary database, Zonda is uniquely positioned to capture trends and changes in the new home market. This report showcases the latest housing trends in the new home market for October 2026. November 20, 2026 – 5 min read Table of Content: The new home market has slipped into underperformance October marked another step backward for the new home market. Sales declined 3.1% month-over-month and 11.7% year-over-year, a considerably steeper annual decline than September's 4.6% drop. The weakness was widespread, with pending sales declining year-over-year across all of Zonda's select markets. The national Zonda Market Ranking also slipped into slightly underperforming territory for the first time since December 2022. The latest figures reinforce what builders have been telling us for months. Zonda's October builder sentiment survey found that 86% of builders reported slower-than-expected demand, up from 84% in September. In their comments, builders pointed to declining traffic, limited buyer urgency, and growing frustration with the effectiveness of incentives. “One of the biggest challenges for builders right now is generating enough buyer interest in the first place,” said Sarah Bonnarens, director of economic research for Zonda and NewHomeSource. “Builders still have an advantage when it comes to pricing and financing flexibility, but those tools can only do so much when buyer traffic is down. The challenge is keeping sales moving without putting even more pressure on margins.” The annual decline in new home sales deepened Zonda's new home sales metric counts the number of new home contract sales each month and accounts for both cancellations and seasonality. This metric shows there were 638,568 new homes sold in October on a seasonally adjusted annualized rate. This was a decline of 3.1% from last month and a drop of 11.7% from a year ago. On a non-seasonally adjusted basis, 50,770 homes were sold, 11.6% lower than last year and 2.8% below the same month in 2019. Incentives remain a key feature of the new home market, helping to sustain sales activity amid ongoing affordability pressures. In October, 64% of new home communities offered incentives on to-be-built homes and 83% on quick move-in supply. Note, these are only publicly available incentives so they will underrepresent overall usage. All select markets saw PSI fall YOY Zonda's New Home Pending Sales Index (PSI) was created to help account for fluctuations in supply by combining both total sales volume with the average sales rate per month per community. The October PSI came in at 122.8, representing an 11.4% decline from the same month last year. The index is currently 29.5% below cycle highs. On a month-over-month basis, seasonally adjusted new home sales decreased 1.9%. The markets that held up the best relative to last year were Minneapolis (-0.3%), Charlotte (-1.1%), and Tampa (-3.5%). Minneapolis was down compared to the last year but grew 10.2% month-over-month. Inversely, the metros that performed the worst year-over-year were Los Angeles/OC (-31.4%), Riverside/San Bernardino (-28.4%), and Denver (-26.3%). On a monthly basis, Minneapolis, Sacramento, and Denver were the best performing markets. The National ZMR dropped to slightly underperforming In order to add further context to sales, Zonda created the Zonda Market Ranking (ZMR). The ZMR accounts for both sales pace and volume, is seasonally adjusted, and is taken as a percentage relative to a baseline market average. Based on the percentage above or below baseline, markets are bucketed into performance groups ranging from significantly underperforming to significantly overperforming relative to historical activity. The map below shows a snapshot of top production markets by region. Zonda also offers the ZMR for entry-level, move-up/move-down, and high-end markets. Subscribers of the National Outlook report can access all top markets and the tiered breakdown in Zonda’s portal. Non-subscribers can access the tiered maps for the select 10 markets by clicking below. Get ZMR Maps The National ZMR index came in at 87.4 in October, which indicated a slightly underperforming market. This marked the first downgrade to the national overall rating since January 2025. Zonda’s snapshot markets were split between 0% overperforming, 10% average, and 90% underperforming. Among Zonda’s top 55 major markets, 5% were overperforming , 25% were average , and 70% were underperforming . Importantly, the ZMR does not account for what it takes to sell a home. For example, securing a sale might still feel difficult in a significantly overperforming market, but if the incentives offered result in a sale, we count the sale. Price cuts persist in the two lower tiers National home prices increased 2.7% year-over-year for high-end homes to $951,036. Prices fell 2.6% for entry-level to $316,019 and 0.5% for move-up to $515,075. The increase in high-end prices reflects, in part, new communities opening at higher price points, often featuring larger homesites, bigger floor plans, and more desirable locations. Meanwhile, modest declines in the entry-level and move-up segments come as builders continue to adjust pricing and product offerings in response to affordability challenges and softer demand. Supplementing our data with a survey Zonda conducts monthly, 43% of builders lowered prices in October month-over-month, 54% held prices flat, and 3% raised prices. In September, for comparison, 38% of builders lowered prices, 52% held prices flat, and 10% increased prices. Community count remained above 18,000 There are currently 18,159 actively selling communities tracked by Zonda, up 6.7% from last year. On a month-over-month basis, the national figure grew 0.6%.
